title: Federal Judge Strikes Down Trump's 75-Country Immigrant Visa Ban as 'Patently Unlawful'
excerpt: A Manhattan judge ruled the State Department's blanket freeze on immigrant visas from 75 nations violated federal law by overriding consular officers' individual case reviews.
body:
• U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas struck down the State Department's policy suspending immigrant visas from 75 countries, calling it "patently unlawful."
  • The January 2026 policy blocked mostly family-based and some employment-based green card applicants from countries across Africa, South Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean.
  • The ruling reversed any visa denial based solely on the policy, though denials on other legal grounds still stand.
  • Pakistan and Bangladesh — countries with large diaspora ties to the Indian-American community — were among the 75 nations affected.

A federal judge in Manhattan on Friday struck down the Trump administration's sweeping ban on immigrant visas from 75 countries, ruling that Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his legal authority by imposing a blanket policy that overrode consular officers' judgment on individual applications.

"The outcome is predetermined," Judge Jeannette Vargas wrote in her decision. "The visa will be refused."

The State Department had paused immigrant visa processing for nearly 40% of the world's nations since January 2026, claiming applicants from those countries posed a "high risk for becoming a public charge" — someone likely to depend on government benefits. The affected countries included Brazil, Colombia, Egypt, Haiti, Somalia, Russia, and several South Asian nations including Pakistan and Bangladesh.

What the Judge Found

Vargas found that the policy violated the Immigration and Nationality Act on two fronts. First, a 1965 provision explicitly bars discrimination by nationality in granting visas. Second, the law strips the secretary of state of authority over how consular officers decide individual visa cases.

A cable Rubio sent to every U.S. diplomatic and consular post, entered into the case record, directed officers to refuse applicants even when someone "provides additional evidence that demonstrates he or she overcomes the public charge refusal." Vargas said this amounted to a categorical prohibition rather than the case-by-case review that federal law requires.

Under existing law, an immigrant can only be turned away as a likely public charge after a consular officer weighs the person's finances, age, health, skills, and family situation — a standard the blanket policy bypassed entirely.

"The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme."

— Judge Jeannette Vargas, U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York

Who Was Affected

The ban targeted permanent-residence visas — green cards for people joining family members or taking jobs in the United States — but did not apply to nonimmigrant visas such as tourist or student visas. Most of the 75 countries were non-European, spanning the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, the Balkans, the Middle East, Central Asia, and Southeast Asia.

Among the plaintiffs were six U.S. citizens who had filed family-based petitions, saying the ban blocked relatives in Ghana, Jamaica, Guatemala, and Ethiopia from obtaining visas. Five Colombians with pending employment-based applications also joined the case.

Impact on Indian Visa Holders

While India was not among the 75 countries on the list, the ruling carries significant weight for the Indian-American community. Pakistan and Bangladesh — nations with deep family and cultural ties across the South Asian diaspora — were directly affected. Immigration attorneys say the decision strengthens legal precedent against nationality-based restrictions, which could matter if the administration attempts similar policies targeting additional countries.

The ruling also follows a separate decision by a Rhode Island judge who struck down related policies freezing work permits, green cards, and other benefits for applicants from roughly 40 travel-ban countries, finding those pauses left many individuals "without work, without legal status, and without any meaningful ability to plan for their futures."

What's Next

The administration won on one narrower point: the judge agreed the policy was not the kind of formal rule that requires public comment before implementation. Vargas gave both sides until September 11 to propose how to resolve the remaining issues in the case. The administration is expected to appeal.

The State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The ruling marks the latest in a string of judicial setbacks for Trump's immigration agenda, which the president has framed as aimed at improving domestic security.
